💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in Latest York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera.
  • Sources indicate that TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year.
  • It has been revealed that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in September, Apple held a photography exhibition in Latest York City to show off the iPhone 18 Pro camera. Now, an image of the Bugaboo Mountains from that exhibit, shot by photographer Jimmy Chin, is included in TIME’s Top 100 Photos.

Sources indicate that TIME publishes its Top 100 Photos list each year. The list showcases the pictures that the TIME Photo Department determines best capture that particular year.

It has been revealed that the essence of TIME’s Photos of the Year, selected by our photo editors and presented below, is the authentic, sometimes staggering, reality captured by photojournalism. Someone was there. A news photographer lifted a viewfinder, pressed a button, and captured an instant happening in front of them.

According to recent reports, chin’s image was shot in Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, on iPhone 18 Pro. He explained that a traditional production creates a layer of separation between the photographer and the subject, with equipment, crew, and all the moving parts of a shoot. Shooting on iPhone 18 Pro meant that he could create a more intimate environment, allowing for a sense of comfort and spontaneity that comes through in the images.

Image Courtesy of Apple (as featured in the What Holds Us exhibition).

Chin’s goal was to capture the intersection of human ambition and the pursuit of wonder against the backdrop of a timeless natural landscape.

Sources indicate that “The resolution and the sharpness on iPhone 18 Pro surprised me. I could shoot a few inches of rock and ice, or a massive panorama, and trust it would hold at size. That is what this work needed. It also meant I carried almost nothing. In the mountains, everything you carry is a decision. I was not thinking about gear. I was thinking about what was in front of me.”.

Apple’s “What Holds Us” exhibit ran in New York City in September, featuring work from photographers Alex Prager, Jack Davison, and Jimmy Chin, with each artist using the iPhone 18 Pro to explore the “people, places, and ideas that connect and ground humanity.” Kathy Ryan, the former longtime director of photography for The New York Times Magazine, curated the exhibition.

Sources indicate that the exhibit is now headed to London, where it will open to the public on December 4, from 10 a.m. to 8 p.m. It will also be open from Saturday, December 12 through Sunday, December 13, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

You can view the full list of this year’s TIME 100 Photos right here.

Industry News: This Hollywood Star Took on Crypto. Now He’s Got a New Target

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous.
  • Turns out, that scene might need an edit.
  • McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben McKenzie promised his wife that he was through with being an activist; that he’d go back to the acting gigs that had made him famous. At the end of his documentary taking on the cryptocurrency industry, Everyone Is Lying to You for Money,” the former star of The O.C. and Gotham turned to his spouse and fellow actor Morena Baccarin and swore he was done.

Turns out, that scene might need an edit. McKenzie is launching a new nonprofit, The Public Trust and Transparency Project, that not only continues his battle with the crypto business but widens it to fight prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi.

McKenzie tells WIRED he’s worried about “the gamification of the economy and the notion that we're turning everything into gambling—both investments, in the form of cryptocurrencies, and “prediction markets,” which look an awful lot like online casinos.”.

In a recent development, “The more gambling gets into our culture, the more people feel like it's somehow a good idea to view these things as legitimate investment strategies,” he says. The prediction markets reject the comparison (although 80 percent of Kalshi’s trades came from sports in September, according to Bloomberg). McKenzie rejects the rejection: “I mean, if your investment strategy is, ‘I'm going to gamble on the Spurs-Knicks,’ like, come on! So there's a real, real problem here.”.

Recent findings suggest that john Reed Stark, who spent 18 years in the Securities and Exchange Commission’s enforcement division, will serve as an adviser to the Project. American Kleptocracy author Casey Michel and Tonantzin Carmona, who runs economic policy for the left-of-center Century Foundation, will sit on the board.

The group is coming together at a time when regulators and law enforcement officials at every level are looking to rein in prediction markets. Federal regulators have launched newly introduced probes into both major prediction markets. The GOP-led House Oversight Committee recently released its investigation into US troops and government insiders trading on insider knowledge on Polymarket and Kalshi. The Senate just passed a bill prohibiting prediction markets for military operations and assassinations. Executives at the markets know they’re in for a rough few months; Kalshi even launched an ad campaign, starring Martha Stewart, reminding its customers not to trade on confidential information.

But insider trading is only one concern among many. There’s also the problem you find in old-school gambling houses too: The vast majority of people who use the markets lose their money. A recent Wall Street Journal report shows that .01 percent of accounts take in two-thirds of all of the profits on Polymarket. On Kalshi, unprofitable accounts outpace profitable ones by almost three to one.

Industry observers note that then there’s the corruption angle, which McKenzie claims is going to be front-and-center for the Project, especially with it featuring as a top matter in the recent midterm elections. Donald Trump Jr. was, until recently, a paid adviser to Kalshi. Trump Jr.’s venture firm, 1789 Capital, made its latest and biggest in a series of investments in Polymarket over the summer; months earlier, the Trump Justice Department sued the state of Minnesota when it tried to ban the prediction markets in the state. (At a recent conference, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called Trump Jr.’s involvement “heavily overblown. We have all types of investors.”).

Prediction markets have been around for hundreds of years, as a forthcoming book on the subject notes. American academics have been turning to them as teaching tools since the late ’80s. Their advocates note that they can be an effective way to hedge against risk, and a form of trading on sports that’s far more consumer-friendly than the online gambling houses. “I accept that there may be some utility,” McKenzie notes. “I'm not saying these things should not exist. I'm just saying they need to be properly regulated.”.

Recent findings suggest that mcKenzie’s plan will be to push Congress in that direction, sort of the inverse of how the former actor lobbied publicly and privately against the “Clarity Act,” which would’ve brought cryptocurrencies into the financial mainstream. (The bill was rejected in September.).

It has been revealed that that pressure is only bound to increase when Democrats take control of Congress next year. “In the bold upcoming world starting [on the] first Monday in January,” Representative Frank Lucas, an Oklahoma Republican, told Politico, “nobody’s untouchable anymore.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CAD images of the iPhone 18e, noted to come from a previously reliable source, have shown a rather odd new design for the camera bump.

If accurate, it would represent a big change from its predecessor, which simply has a single lens protruding without a surrounding bump or plateau ….

The iPhone 17e was rolled out in March with a design unchanged from last year’s iPhone 16e. While the camera did get some feature enhancements, including the ability to store depth information for portrait photos, the physical camera design remained the same.

It has been revealed that the current model has a single lens protruding directly from the casing with a flush-mounted flashlight next to it. Engadget reports on CAD images showing a very different approach with next year’s iPhone 18e.

The renders show an almost square camera bump measuring about 28 mm by 35 mm that houses the single rear camera, the LED flash and the rear microphone.

The site doesn’t share the images, but indicates that the camera bump looks similar to that of the M5 iPad Pro, shown below.

It’s unclear what might have prompted the change of design, especially as the site’s Filipe Espósito says he’s also seen CAD models for the standard model iPhone 18 or the iPhone Air 2, neither of which adopt it.

Previous reports have suggested that the only spec change with the iPhone 18e over its predecessor will be performance improvements thanks to the A20 chip.

Recent findings suggest that that’s a heck of a lot of bonuses. 💡 Key Takeaways

  • Samsung is busy preparing for its next smartphone lineup, the Galaxy S27 Series, and a new leak points to a possible redesign for the Live Notifications view in the Now Bar, which could be moving front and center where the front camera sits.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for years, Apple has taken pages out of Samsung's book when developing its own devices — just look at the iPhone Duo, which arrived seven years after Samsung's first foldable. But oh, how the tables have turned.

Samsung is busy preparing for its next smartphone lineup, the Galaxy S27 Series, and a new leak points to a possible redesign for the Live Notifications view in the Now Bar, which could be moving front and center where the front camera sits. SamMobile spotted the changes while sifting through the One UI 9.5 software.

As it stands, the Now Bar (which displays real-time tools such as timers, map directions, and other ongoing activities) sits in the top-left corner next to the time display. If it looks familiar to you, you're not alone — numerous customers have compared it to Apple's flagship Dynamic Island feature, which was introduced with the iPhone 14 Pro back in 2022.

While the Now Bar is projected for a redesign, its lock screen version is set to remain in its usual position at the bottom-center of the smartphone display.

In a recent development, however, it's not just the design that Samsung is drawing inspiration from Apple. Instead of the current up-and-down swipe navigation you use to view your Live Notifications, the leak reveals a new left-to-right swipe function when flicking through your ongoing activities in its new pill-shaped form, just like the Dynamic Island.

In a recent development, but where Samsung could take it a step further is with a latest Now Bar settings page, which was also spotted in the leaked firmware. As well as the redesign, SamMobile also found 'Moments effects', a new page within the Now Bar where you can download add-on packs that show basic animations.

In a recent development, right now, only the 'Sports' pack is listed as an available add-on, which displays the prompt "Celebrate your favourite teams’ scores and wins. Available for select sports supported by Google Sports". When a team you're tracking via Google Sports scores or wins, it triggers a fun animation that appears in the Now Bar. Though this feature was softly introduced in the One UI 9.5 Beta 1, the leak suggests Samsung has intends to add more categories in the future.

Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android.

Industry observers note that these at-a-glance notification centers are pretty much the new norm with every smartphone release. Though Apple arguably pioneered it a few years ago, countless tech brands have followed suit with their own versions, so it was only a matter of time before Samsung had to bite the bullet.

There's no doubt the Now Bar redesign will be a welcome quality-of-life upgrade, but we won't know anything for certain until Samsung decides when it's the right time to divulge more information.

Your browser does not support the audio element.

It has been revealed that this July, as the Railroad Fire spread through Washington overnight, Watch Duty sent its first-ever nighttime Critical Alert to its users. It started with a 911 dispatch buried in radio static — and a newly introduced Gemini tool that caught it in seconds.

According to recent reports, A dedicated team of Google engineers and researchers spent six months embedded full-time with Watch Duty, a nonprofit wildfire alert app run by active and retired firefighters, dispatchers, and first responders. Through the Google.org Fellowship, they used more than 20,000 hours of past radio recordings to build a Gemini-powered tool that wipes out heavy static and translates specialized firefighting terminology into clean, searchable text. The system removes the added strain of deciphering noisy audio so volunteers can focus on verifying incidents and getting alerts out.

Recent findings suggest that when a wildfire starts, minutes can decide whether people get out safely. Yet across much of the country, the first word of a new fire still travels over decades-old analog VHF radio, where engine noise, wind, static, and rapid-fire tactical jargon make it hard to hear what's happening. Watch Duty reporters monitor up to 20 feeds manually, making it a challenge to cut through the noise.

Across Watch Duty's network, the tool has:.

As a result of the collaboration between Google and Watch Duty, volunteer reporter satisfaction with radio transcription tools increased from 35.3% to 92.3%.

The tool was also put to test during a live fire. In July 2026, a fast-moving wildfire — the Railroad Fire — ignited at night in Washington. When the first 911 dispatch went out over local fire radio, the Gemini-powered transcription tool transcribed it straight from the noisy radio audio and flagged it in under 30 seconds.

That head start gave Watch Duty's team the time they needed to verify the fire and push a Critical Alert—which breaks through do-not-disturb mode in urgent situations—helping residents evacuate before flames reached homes. It was the first time Watch Duty had ever sent a Critical Alert overnight, proving what faster detection means when communities are asleep and every minute counts.

The newly introduced AI radio tool is the latest milestone in a deep, multi-year collaboration spanning Google's philanthropic, product, and research teams to help Watch Duty scale its life-saving mission across all 50 states.

When the next fire starts, the goal is simple: get people the warning they need while there's still time to act.

Frontier AI models that have yet to be released by OpenAI and Anthropic are reportedly reaching the point where employees believe they cannot be safely released or controlled, employees reportedly say.

Axios cites “more than two dozen” employees inside of OpenAI and Anthropic who are sounding warnings around unreleased models from both companies.

According to recent reports, while both OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude public models are increasingly powerful, these employees say that newly introduced models behind the scenes are starting to beat out the technical solutions for controlling them. This has led to debates between those who think they’ll be able to fix these problems, and others who believe companies should stop training new models altogether due to the risks.

According to recent reports, if we continue trying to make models much smarter, such that they’re actually smarter than us … they will in fact be able to trick us successfully. And once you get to that point, many of the schemes that we’ve had at work up until now sort of go out the window.

The report goes out to point out that some researchers feel that executives at major AI companies have become “out of touch” with the severity of safety risks, though Axios was told that OpenAI is adopting upcoming safety practices while Anthropic noted that “Keeping a model internal doesn’t make it safe,” adding that “we may slow down or hold back even when it costs us.”.

IHOP is officially entering the holiday merch wars, but keeping supplies super thin.

Starting Nov. 30, IHOP is launching its inaugural Collector’s Holiday Mug for $15 at participating restaurants nationwide. The catch? Each IHOP location is receiving just 24 mugs for the entire holiday season, making this the first-ever branded merchandise item sold inside IHOP dining rooms.

At just $15, it undercuts virtually every rival coffeehouse collector mug on the market, including the fresh Starbucks FriendsWithYou ceramic mug. And you're not forced to buy a pricey combo meal or download a loyalty app just to unlock access.

The real matter is that 24 mugs per restaurant is virtually nothing.

Once the first 24 mugs at your local IHOP sell out on Nov. 30, they are gone for good. There are no online restocks, no mobile-order reservations, and no second shipments scheduled for December. If you genuinely want one for your shelf or a holiday gift, you will need to visit a participating restaurant in person right when doors open on Nov. 30. The only alternative is to pay obnoxious reseller markups, and nobody wants that.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the debate over the wisdom and safety of using Meta’s Muse AI agent continues as the app rolls out in the UK. It follows a warning by a number of regulatory bodies about the potential risks of AI agents ….

Meta yesterday revealed the UK availability of Muse.

Muse, Meta’s personal Al agent, is now available to adults in the UK. Think of it as a helping hand for the jobs that pile up, like chasing a refund, renewing car insurance or keeping on top of the school calendar. To get those jobs done you can connect Muse to the apps you already use, from your email and calendar to the retailer apps you shop on.

A forum representing four different UK regulatory bodies last month issued a warning about the potential dangers involved in using AI agents. The Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum said:.

AI agents may amplify and accelerate risks and introduce latest ones. These risks may increase as the capabilities of personal agents grow and adoption rises. Questions of consumer protection, competition and data protection – for example the risk of fraud and scams, personal information sharing not in line with user expectations and misleading recommendations, decisions or information provided – must be addressed to ensure innovation develops in ways that earn and maintain public trust.

Meta has pushed back against suggestions that Muse has accessed personal data without permission, insisting that customers are in control and must approve important actions. The organization has admitted to some “isolated incidents,” but notes other reported breaches were either hallucinations or took place on internal versions of the app while undergoing testing. In a new blog post, Meta says:.

Recent findings suggest that muse only works with the apps and services you choose to connect it to, and you control the access it gets […] Once you’ve decided what Muse is connected to and what you want it to do, with your oversight, it can handle tasks like searching, comparing and planning for you. But before it does anything like sending an email or buying something, it demonstrates you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your go-ahead. A separate security agent checks Muse’s actions and the information it sends out against the permissions you’ve granted. You can also choose how often it checks in with you in Settings.

At the time of writing, Muse remains the second most popular free app in Apple’s US App Store, with more than 10 million downloads. We reported yesterday that some banks are already blocking AI agents, while others are warning that they will not be responsible for the consequences of any actions taken by them.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Following its debut on the Galaxy Watch 9 earlier this year, Samsung is finally rolling out Wear OS 7 to older Galaxy Watch models with its One UI 9 Watch update.

Samsung’s One UI 9 Watch update is largely focused on new health features including Vitals, Heart Health Score, Daily Cardio Load, Fitness Index, and improvements to both Sleep Coaching and Sleep Apnea alerts.

“Vitals” is perhaps the most useful day-to-day addition, with Samsung Health collecting data on key vital signs such as heart rate, heart rate variability, respiratory rate, skin temperature, and blood oxygen and establishing a range so you can see when your vitals are out of the usual range.

One UI 9 Watch is based on Wear OS 7, and also includes an improved Compass app with “Track Back,” a feature that helps people to follow their route back to a recorded point.

There’s also a latest “Portrait Watch Face” that can adjust the clock face around the subject of a photo.

Recent findings suggest that samsung is, as of today, officially rolling out One UI 9 Watch with Wear OS 7 to the Galaxy Watch 8 and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. Meanwhile, the patch is in beta for several other older models which will be updated soon including:.

The Galaxy Watch 5 series and Watch FE should also be getting the revision, but no beta is available for those devices. Samsung’s first Wear OS watches, the Galaxy Watch 4 series, will not get the update.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.
  • Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how consumers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.
  • iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Since iOS 5 in 2011, the iPhone and iPad have included Notification Center, a central place to find alerts from various apps in chronological order.

Starting with iOS 27, Apple is making a major change to how consumers open Notification Center on iPhone and iPad.

iOS 27 is here after a summer of beta releases. The behavior changed slightly between the first two releases. However, this change shipped, and I’m still adjusting to it.

Opening Notification Center is unchanged on iOS 27 and iPadOS 27 by default. However, enabling Siri AI changes a key swipe gesture on both iPhone and iPad.

One of the many ways of invoking Siri AI, once enabled, is by swiping down from the center of the top edge of your iPhone or iPad display. This previously opened Notification Center.

You can still access Notification Center by swiping down from the top-left corner once Siri AI is enabled. Alerts now animate in from the top left corner. This is a way to point users toward Notification Center’s smaller surface area.

According to recent reports, apple is greatly prioritizing Siri AI access in iOS 27. The majority of the top edge is devoted to invoking the fresh Siri experience.

It has been revealed that the last time Apple made a change to accessing Notification Center came when Control Center moved from a swipe up gesture from the bottom to a top-right corner swipe down gesture on iPhone X. Apple later unified this experience across devices.

Recent findings suggest that now it’s Notification Center’s turn to be put in the corner. On iPadOS 27 beta 1 in particular, the area above Home screen app icons was pretty much devoted to invoking Siri AI. The area for opening Notification Center actually shrank if you disable displaying AM/PM or the date.

It has been revealed that I've been always swiping from the left corner to see my notifications. I didn't even know you could swipe from the center to get to it as well 😂 I guess I'm good then?

Apple improved this with iPadOS 27 beta 2, creating a more uniform region on either side. It’s roughly the size of two app columns with Notification Center on the left and Control Center on the right. The rest is for invoking Siri.

After 15 years of muscle memory, it’ll take some time to determine if this change is worth it or something that should be reconsidered. In the meantime, early feedback sounds overwhelmingly positive around Apple’s fresh Siri AI system. Hearing that Siri is good now will also take some getting used to, I’m sure.

After months of using the newly introduced behavior, I’m certain I’d toggle it off if there were a setting to do so. Since there’s no option to disable invoking Siri from the top middle swipe down, the only thing to do is build new muscle memory around avoiding the center.

It has been revealed that what do you think? Would you change this back if you could? Is accessing Siri from the swipe-down gesture worth the change? Share your thoughts in the comments.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you've been looking for a compact Android tablet that can compete with Apple's iPad mini, the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is arguably one of the best options out there. While the tablet is a little expensive at its usual $900 price, Lenovo's flagship gaming tablet is now down to just $600, saving you a massive $300 (33%).

Industry observers note that the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 packs flagship-level performance into a compact tablet with an 8.8-inch 165Hz display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, 12GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and a massive 9,000mAh battery. It's now $300 off ahead of Black Friday.

✅Recommended if: You want a compact Android tablet with flagship performance, a high refresh rate display, and excellent battery capacity for gaming, watching movies, or traveling.

❌Skip this deal if: You prefer a larger screen for productivity, specifically want an OLED display, or only need a basic tablet for browsing and streaming.

Recent findings suggest that one of my favorite things about the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is its form factor. There aren't many compact Android tablets on the market that offer flagship-level specs, but the Legion Tab Gen 5 manages to pack some pretty powerful hardware into a device with an 8.8-inch display.

And while it uses an IPS LCD panel rather than an AMOLED display, it supports a refresh rate of up to 165Hz, which is considerably higher than the 60Hz display you get on the iPad mini.

It has been revealed that but the biggest reason to consider the Legion Tab Gen 5 is its performance. The tablet is powered by Qualcomm's Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chipset, paired with 12GB of RAM and 256GB of onboard storage. Even though it's no longer Qualcomm's latest flagship chipset, it's still one of the most powerful processors you'll find in an Android tablet.

Lenovo has also managed to pack a massive 9,000mAh battery into this compact tablet, which should give you plenty of gaming time without having to constantly reach for a charger.

And even if you're not particularly into gaming, I think the Legion Tab Gen 5 makes for a pretty great travel companion. Its 8.8-inch display is big enough to comfortably watch movies, read books, or browse the web on a long flight, but the tablet itself is still compact enough to carry around without taking up much space in your backpack.

On the whole, if you've been waiting for a proper Android alternative to the iPad mini that doesn't compromise on performance, the Lenovo Legion Tab Gen 5 is definitely worth checking out. Its usual $900 price makes it a little difficult to recommend, but at $600, it's a much more compelling option.

Wyze is today launching the Window Bird Cam, a newly introduced $70 camera that has a bird feeder and can identify bird species, keep a log, and more.

In a recent development, the Wyze Window Bird Cam comes in two parts. There’s a stick-up camera that mounts to the inside of your window with a shade to reduce reflections, similar to the Wyze Window Cam that debuted last year. The other half mounts to the outside of your window with suction cups and includes a tray for birdseed.

The idea here is to attract birds direct to the camera’s view, with Wyze further adding a new “Bird Watch” feature to its app which can identify bird species and keep a log of what species have stopped by and how many birds are using the feeder.

According to recent reports, the camera’s lens is tuned for focus distances of around 4-6 inches and has a higher frame rate of 30fps. The feeder tray has drainage and there’s an add-on perch for $15 extra.

In a recent development, “Bird Watch” is free for 3 months, but costs $6.99/month (or $69.99/year) after that. Free owners still get live view and bird detection, but no species ID, a limited log, and no cloud recordings of bird visits (there is a microSD card slot for local recording).

#3476. Latest Update: 8 Best Espresso Machines for Home (2026), Tested by Coffee Pros

📅 11 Oct 2021 • ⏱️ 28m • 📚 Deep Dive (5659 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 8 Best Espresso Machines for Home (2026), Tested by Coffee Pros

📅 11 Oct 2021 | ⏱️ 28 min read (5659 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~28 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle.
  • Sources indicate that I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup.
  • But I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Best espresso machines for home must thread a delicate needle. Espresso is forceful and finicky, and a little intimidating, and yet so essential that astronauts might take it into orbit. A home espresso machine remains the most intense and expensive device I regularly operate before my first cup of coffee.

Sources indicate that I tend to favor devices that let technology do much of the work and don’t make you join a cult of engineers before your first cup. And so my top-rated espresso machine, the Fellow Series 1, earned its place on WIRED’s counter by combining ease of use with a solid build, consistent temperature, and rare control over pressure—an industry-beating mix of nerdiness and hand-holding friendliness. For a more classic, all-analog build, we offer the compact, stylish Diletta Mio.

But I know not everyone wants to also buy a good coffee grinder or spend four figures for their morning cup. For those who want milk-based drinks and a built-in grinder, I recommend the top-selling Breville Barista Express as the Goldilocks machine balancing performance and cost. For an entry-level device, I pretty much always recommend the straight-ahead Breville Bambino, among the lowest-cost machines with PID-controlled temperature.

Note that this guide mostly covers classic, hands-on espresso machines with portafilters. We do also include the De'Longhi Rivelia, our top pick among super-automatic espresso machines that require little more than a button press. For a guide that focuses on easy-to-use espresso machine picks that do most of the work for you, check out our guide to the Best Latte and Automatic Espresso Machines.

Also, be sure to check out our other coffee guides, like the Best Drip Coffee Makers, Best Cold Brew Makers, Best Aeropresses, Best Coffee Pod Machines, Best Coffee Subscriptions, and Best Coffee Grinders.

Updated November 2026: We’ve added information on Meraki’s second-run release and ensured up-to-date links and prices.

San Francisco-based Fellow is almost certainly the most innovative and tech-forward coffee machine manufacturer of the moment. And rarely has an espresso machine so swiftly changed what I want from the best espresso makers as the Fellow Series 1, which started shipping in early 2026. Sure, the temperature control is admirable, with a patented heating technology that threads the needle between the fast heating of a thermoblock and the stability of a boiler. Automatic milk frothing is about as good and as fast as it gets. The dial and LED-screen controls are intuitive. And the device is compact, conserving both counter space and airspace.

But the real game-changing addition with this machine is the way Fellow has introduced tight pressure control and shot profiles to the non-geek home espresso landscape. Almost every other espresso machine on the market just sorta aims at 9 bars of pressure and shrugs. The Series 1 offers profiles for light, medium, or dark roast that change pressure based on what's right for each bean—keeping dark roasts classic but pulling longer shots and dialing back pressure on light-roast beans. Other profiles, like turbo shots or “Modern Arc,” cater to the modern yen for espresso with less bitterness.

In a recent development, after testing for weeks, I'm sold. You'd pay at least double to find this feature on any other espresso machine. And no device lets you play with pressure as easily as the Fellow, even before a planned firmware upgrade that'll allow you to sync profiles through Fellow's phone app. The app remains mostly a placeholder for now, offering tutorials and education but TBD functionality. But Fellow's track record building out the app on my top-pick drip coffee machine, the Fellow Aiden, gives me confidence this is a temporary blip. Volumetric controls still need tweaking, and the removable water reservoir can only be removed straight up from the device, requiring significant clearance.

But even with these early quirks, the Fellow Series 1 remains the most impressive espresso machine I've tested in the past couple of years. And it's changed what I want from espresso machines in the future. The Series 1 might already be the most-hyped machine of 2026. But this time, the hype is warranted.

Sources indicate that the Barista Express had been our top pick for years, a Goldilocks choice in terms of price, versatility, and performance. It remains among the most popular espresso machines in the world (and possibly the most popular, period) for good reason. The Barista Express produces consistent pressure for espresso, its steam wand is excellent, and the built-in grinder makes it an all-in-one device. Its mostly metal construction, easy cleaning, and other thoughtful touches make it a faithful companion. My WIRED colleague Julian Chokkattu has been using his machine happily for seven years. And its price, which drops regularly during sales events, makes it accessible to mere mortals. For those who want a built-in grinder but don't want to spend four figures, this is an easy recommendation.

Industry observers note that competitors have taken direct aim at the Express with impressive semiautomatic entries like the Ninja Luxe Cafe Premier ($599) and Luxe Cafe Pro (see below), plus the De'Longhi La Specialista Opera ($900). Each of these offers more options, including cold espresso, with similar grind quality. For now, WIRED's years of testing and vetting the Barista Express, and Breville's good customer service reputation, keep the Express as my top recommendation. But in the meantime, I wouldn't be sad to see the Barista Express updated to better Baratza burrs on that built-in grinder, as Breville has done with its more expensive machines.

Upgrade pick: The Barista Express is a great mix of price and performance. But Breville's true top-line semiautomatic machine is the Breville Oracle Jet ($1,980 on Amazon), a touchscreen device with a better grinder that'll also offer better control and easier milk frothing and can guide you through everything from the proper bean grind to how to make a proper flat white, cappuccino, or espresso martini.

Recent findings suggest that A classic espresso machine rewards effort with nuance and beauty. And the Diletta Mio is everything a classic Italian-made espresso machine should be. It's compact, stylish, built to last, and brews circles around the competition. It's also a simple joy to use, wrote former WIRED reviewer Jaina Grey. It feels a bit analog, like an heirloom-quality stand mixer, but also sports sophisticated features like a PID (proportional-integral-derivative) temperature controller—a wee processor with an algorithm that keeps brew temperatures stable. Among traditional espresso machines that require a separate grinder, this is the one WIRED recommends.

According to recent reports, upgrade: WIRED's upgrade pick, the Diletta Bello ($1,899), is for advanced beanheads who love a sensitive machine. On the Bello, every difference makes a difference: every micron of grind size, or slight gradation of tamping pressure, will produce a different cup of espresso. But when you've dialed in your bean, the Bello is beautifully faithful—offering shot after shot of caramely crema and rich espresso.

It has been revealed that the Bambino is little, fast, low-cost, and convenient—about as wide as a one-dollar bill. There are no apparent frills and no grinder: just a steam wand for silky milk and a choice between single or double shots. But look under the hood of this $300 beauty and you'll note features that are hallmarks of much more expensive machines: a thermoblock for immediate heating and a PID (proportional, integral, derivative) temperature controller that makes for consistent brew temps usually out of reach at this price range.

Which is to say it's a wee machine that pulls far above its weight class. Pair your Bambino with a good mid-level grinder and you'll be making beautiful cups with counter space to spare, for a total of $500.

Upgrade: The Breville Bambino Plus ($500) is hardier and slightly bigger and offers automatic milk frothing.

It has been revealed that the Rancilio Silvia Pro is one of WIRED's longtime favorite dual-boiler espresso machines, packed with pro-level features and built to last seemingly forever, with few plastic parts. For far less than half the price, there's the Silvia M: the sleek, smaller-footprint, single-boiler cousin. What's the diff? There'll be a little bit more lag time between shots, if multiple people want espresso immediately. But you'll get that same high-quality metal build, and consistent water temp and steam pressure. This means well-extracted, café-grade espresso.

It has been revealed that note that the Silvia is notoriously sensitive, so it's not for beginners. It's also famously long-lasting, repairable, and able to be endlessly modified, and so it's birthed its own society of cult devotees. Just like buying a Land Cruiser or a Jeep, you'll end up with newly introduced friends. And if people online are to be believed, a lot of the OG Silvias have been chugging along for literal decades.

Sources indicate that it's tough to find a reliable espresso machine in the $200 range—and Italian coffee machine company De'Longhi has long dominated the WIRED Gear team's favorite no-nonsense, low-budget espresso picks. The new De'Longhi Classic (previously branded as “Linea Classic”) is shiny chrome, with buttons for steam and your choice of single or double shots. It likewise sports a rare-at-this-price-point pressure gauge, a 15-bar pump, and an updated thermoblock system for fast heating.

Industry observers note that the small touches matter. The steam wand has enough oomph to create some rudimentary latte art, if that’s your thing. And there's enough clearance between the portafilter and drip tray to fit a coffee or cappuccino mug, as opposed to a tiny espresso cup. But this said, after learning a few fun tricks from coffee influencer Lance Hedrick, I'm now also revisiting our previous extreme budget pick, De'Longhi Stilosa.

In a recent development, this guide is mostly dedicated to machines that make more classic espresso—the finicky kind that's harder to navigate and might leave coffee grounds on your counter. This sophisticated bean-to-cup De'Longhi Rivelia is a little different. It's my top pick among super-automatic machines that'll have you just fill a hopper with a half-bag of beans, then press a button. After helping you choose the right grinder settings, and asking how you like your coffee among well more than a dozen options, this touchscreen device will grind, and brew, and then froth up your milk for you.

Even the milk frother is about the easiest I've used, and it works with a single button-press once you've adjusted the foam density for drinks from dense flat white to frothy cappuccino. Heck, my mom was able to figure it out within a day, and so was my father. Even better, the Rivelia offers two swappable bean hoppers, an unheard-of luxury among similar devices that'll allow you to switch easily to decaf late in the day.

Recent findings suggest that note, however, that automatic machines like this Rivelia tend to make somewhat different coffee from what you'll get from other machines on this list. It grinds a bit coarser, leading to less unpredictability but also less intensity. If you're a milk lover, this likely won't matter much—and you may instead prize the simple ease with which you can have a frothing latte. Vodka lovers will find the same, when mixing cold espresso shots with the device.

Ever wonder why an espresso shot is sometimes called a pull? In the beginning, baristas used a lever to create the necessary pressure to extract espresso. And there's still a real satisfaction to literally pulling your own espresso, reviewer Jaina Grey noted. There’s no milk steamer, no boiler, no power cable. This thing is powered by a human, namely you.

Load it up with coffee and water per the manufacturer’s instructions and give it a good press. There’s also a pressure gauge to make sure you're hitting the target. Think of it like one of those strongman games at a carnival, except that the reward is delicious espresso.

How Do I Test Espresso Machines?

Industry observers note that over the past decade, WIRED has tested dozens of espresso makers to find our favorites. The process, in part, is simple. We brew a whole lot of coffee. I’ve written about coffee for more than a decade on both the East and West Coasts, including my hometown coffee mecca of Portland, Oregon. Other current and past WIRED espresso testers—who include former baristas and longtime coffee writers—include Jaina Grey, Jeffrey Van Camp, Kat Merck, Tyler Shane, Pete Cottell, and Scott Gilbertson.

Sources indicate that on each machine that’s capable, I make and assess at least four styles of drink, on multiple roasts and beans: a basic 2:1 espresso, an Americano, a latte, and a cappuccino. On machines that advertise a wacky array of drinks, I test each one. This includes any newfangled coldspresso and head-scratching variations on a “long.” It also includes, if science dictates, espresso martinis. And I test to see whether a machine can be dialed to both dark roasts and lighter roasts.

I might make many dozens of coffees to dial in a machine and truly understand it, and on any of my top picks I've made at least fifty drinks. Sometimes, alas, you understand a machine’s shortcomings far sooner—and so some of our less-recommended devices are dismissed a bit earlier.

What I’m looking for is nuance, aromatics, beauty, sensitivity to the characteristics of each bean, and the satisfying texture of fully integrated milk. But also, I’m looking for ease, the thoughtful touches that make an espresso maker something you can fall in love with.

I test whether the hot water spout splatters, whether descaling requires a degree in hydrology, whether the brewing temperature is consistent, and whether the latte milk gets silked. I’m truly terrible at latte art, but whether it’s possible is a straightforward test of the body of the frothed milk. I test the airier foam of cappuccinos and compare manual and automatic milk frothing on machines that try to froth milk for you. I test how fast the wand steams and whether it’s easy to fully integrate milk before the dang thing starts to burn your milk.

On machines with built-in grinders, I both assess the grind and weigh the dose—and then weigh it again. And then again. Consistency is the hobgoblin of little cups. I also test multiple grind settings to make sure the grind is consistent.

It has been revealed that on any semiautomatic machine that decides the shot size for you, I test this to see whether you're getting a ristretto or a lungo by default. Then I resolve never to say the word “lungo” again.

I don’t generally take apart the machines I’m sent, but I do quite often look up videos of people who do—and look at how the thing’s constructed under the hood.

How I Select Espresso Machines to Review.

In part, we select machines to test by looking at the espresso makers with long track records of making good espresso machines—people with long tails in the industry and good track records of customer support. Names like Breville, De'Longhi, La Marzocco, and Rancilio. But also, I listen. I read. I ask every coffee-obsessive in my life. I pay attention to the newest releases, follow trade shows, watch Youtube videos, and spend a lot of time tracking down not just the obious big names but the unexpected recommendations.

I often also look at how accessible each machine will be to most people. Espresso isn’t just a finicky process: It’s finicky by design. The most sensitive and sophisticated traditional machines are responsive to every tiny variation in the coffee grind and every fluctuation in the water temperature. The deepest bean geeks want this: They want the control, the frustration, the vision quest.

In a recent development, but I also know that most of you out there aren’t looking to be in an abusive relationship with your coffee machine. Few want to wake up to feelings of inadequacy, brought on by a machine that costs as much as a used car. And so what I look for is the espresso machines that can pull lovely character from each bean, but also make this easy on you.

Recent findings suggest that this means that our top picks, the ones I recommend to most people, tend to fall in the semiautomatic camp: They’re the ones that offer the best coffee with the least effort. Finding this balance is delicate and often rewarding. It used to be that a built-in grinder was a recipe for blown shots, sadness, or pressurized portafilters with less character. But year by year, espresso machine makers get better at this goal.

The lowest-cost machines I recommend tend to offer more forgiving pressurized filter baskets as options, even though these sacrifice a bit of nuance for forgiveness, because I don’t want to assume you’re pairing a $200 espresso machine with a $2,000 coffee grinder. Although I know some of you do this, especially with our beloved Breville Bambino.

But hey, if you’re a tinkerer for life, and want to join modding groups? We recommend a machine for you, too. Mostly so you can disagree on Reddit, and explain why your favorite is better.

What Beans Are Best for Espresso?

Sources indicate that first off, there's no such thing as “espresso beans,” whatever it says on the bag you buy. Espresso beans are coffee beans, ground finely enough to be pressed into service as espresso.

Sources indicate that but traditionally, espresso is made with darker-roast beans that best elicit the deep, chocolatey notes of classic Italian espresso. In fact, most machines you use are probably designed with dark-roast beans in mind: Darker beans grind easier, extract easier, and are a bit more homogeneous across the market. And so when someone writes “espresso roast” or “espresso blend” on their grind, that's often what they mean.

Recent findings suggest that does that mean dark roast is the only espresso? Of course not. Modern craft and premium coffee roasters in the United States have begun trending toward medium and medium-dark roasts that offer a bit more balance, character, and even a little acidity—beans that have more aromatics, and more individuality. Some, including me, love experimenting with truly light roasts, including the lightest of natural-processed beans that let me brew up espresso that tastes like strawberries.

It's up to you. But note that the lighter the roast, the more you'll need to adjust grind and temperature to accommodate—and sometimes even go off-script entirely. (See here for an explainer on light-roast espresso.) But the classic recommendations for espresso? Pulling a 25- to 30-second shot, at a steady 9 bars of pressure, at a 2:1 ratio for a standard shot? These were all designed for traditional dark-roast beans.

One thing that's true, however, is that you should use fresh beans. They'll taste better and more aromatic, sure. But stale beans exposed to oxygen also make it technically difficult to make good espresso: they've begun to break down, often allow channeling, and are more likely to lead to a less evenly extracted shot with funny off-flavors.

Recent findings suggest that obviously, fresh beans are easiest to obtain from a local roaster, and on the plus side you'll be able to ask the baristas there how best to make espresso from their beans. But when in doubt in a supermarket, look for a roast date on the bag. If you can't find it, or if your beans were roasted in Italy and sent on a ship? Chances are they're not fresh. And your espresso will be worse. For fresh beans delivered to your house, check out WIRED's guide to the best coffee subscriptions.

Espresso Accessories That Make for Great Cups.

If you're spending this much on an espresso machine, you'll want to invest in a good grinder and even a scale, as well as a few other devices that make your shots better, and your life a little easier.

Industry observers note that an espresso-capable grinder: If your espresso machine doesn't come with a grinder, you'll need one. Preground bag beans are especially difficult to use when making espresso, and will likely lead to off-flavors or channeling. But not just any grinder will do. You'll need a good grinder that can grind consistent beans finely enough for espresso. WIRED's top-pick Baratza Encore ESP is always a good choice—positioned squarely at the fulcrum where more expensive grinders begin to offer diminishing returns.

An accurate scale with a timer: Most grinders, and a goodly portion of espresso machines, do not offer a precise scale. But a precise scale is what you need to get espresso ratios right. WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu loved the Acaia brew-by-weight scale ($400) that automatically connects to the La Marzocco Linea Mini and a few other devices via its companion app. But a far less sophisticated scale can still help you measure your shot size and control the dose you want on each espresso shot. If you're not precious about beauty, there's always this low-cost, little no-name scale. It's accurate to a 10th of a gram, and has a timer to boot.

The best knockbox: When you're done with that portafilter filled with coffee grounds, what do you do with it? Beat it against the side of a trashcan? Dig out those grounds into the sink? Nah. You need a good knock box. And somehow this jobby-job from Breville is the best one I've ever found. It's sturdy, the cross bar is in the right spot so that the grinds dump cleanly into the bin, and the bottom has enough grip that the box doesn't scoot around on the counter. Simplicity is competence.

Not all steaming pitchers are created equal, notes WIRED contributing reviewer (and former barista) Pete Cottell. As opposed to the sad piece of aluminum that probably came with your espresso maker, this Brewista offers thick walls for heat retention, a precision tip for expert latte pours, and a thermometer sticker on its side so you can get a rough gauge of milk temperature without hunting down an actual thermometer. It can also take a beating. This is your upcoming frothing pitcher.

Breville Oracle Jet for $2,000: The Breville Oracle Jet is my previous top pick for threading that delicate needle between ease and deliciousness, before getting displaced by my new top-pick Fellow device. The Oracle Jet remains a powerful and frankly beautiful stainless-steel machine, with sterling temperature control and a solid built-in grinder that uses the same conical burrs as the excellent Baratza Encore ESP ($200). This Oracle Jet will pull beautiful nuances from beans ranging from berry-light to chocolate dark, on drinks ranging from an Americano to a flat white to “cold espresso” best placed in a martini. And yet the Jet's easily accessible for anyone who can figure out an iPhone, with a touchscreen tutorial, digital guidance on finding the right grind for each bean, and automatic tamping and steaming. You'll be nose-deep in a cappuccino within 20 minutes of pulling this thing out of the box. Note that manual milk steaming with the Jet's powerful wand is still better than the automatic version.

Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro for $750: Tradition is the opposite of what Ninja does. This is the firm that made the soft-serve Swirl, the Slushi, and the portable air fryer. Ninja is all about the extras. And Ninja doesn't judge. And so of course Ninja jumped in with both feet on cold-foam coldspresso. In fact, the fresh Luxe Cafe Pro makes the best cold foam out of any espresso machine I've tried, with a whisk that whips up plant milk or cow milk into thick, creamy, dense, beautiful froth—ready for your ridiculously complicated cold caramel-vanilla latte TikTok recipe. What I didn't expect was that Ninja would also nail the fundamentals so well, on only its second entry into the espresso market. The relatively accurate by-weight dosing is nice. So is the excellent steam wand that also outpaces most contenders on automatic hot foaming, adjustable to multiple densities of foam. The Pro clears up some oversights in the previous-model Premier, including an easy tamping lever, and a hot water spout. Maintenance, whether descaling or purging, is also as easy as it gets. Just don't use this grinder with light roast beans. Medium or dark only.

Breville Oracle Dual Boiler for $3,000: This update to the previous Breville Dual Boiler espresso machine is a powerful, truly impressive machine in many regards. It combines the easy touchscreen operation and automatic dosing and tamping of WIRED's previous top-pick Oracle Jet with a welcome “manual” mode that lets you play with pre-infusion and bloom while monitoring a digital pressure gauge on the touchscreen. I kinda love this as an exercise in future-retro design—or whatever the inverse of steampunk is—but also as a means of really controlling my shot, and getting a lot more crema and body out of it. The dual boiler heats up very fast—like four minutes fast—and gives you the wonderful temperature stability and consistency you expect from a dual boiler, plus the ability to steam milk and make espresso simultaneously. The production model I received had a very tight portafilter fit, which loosened up after the first 30 shots or so but initially required some muscle. I also haven't been able to get good results with lighter-roast beans, which led to the occasional under-filled portafilter that had to be retamped manually. We'll update as we resolve those quirks, but can attest that for medium to dark beans, this Dual Boiler is an absolute beast.

Industry observers note that meraki Espresso Machine for $1,999: When former WIRED reviewer Matthew Korfhage first tested this high-design “steampunk gasworks” of an espresso machine, he loved the features for the price, including a Timemore grinder that grinds by weight, PID temperature control, easy pre-infusion, and another scale under the brewer that lets you control output. He did not, however, love having to overrotate the portafilter for a proper fit, or the wackily complicated descaling procedure. I’ve since tested the second run of this machine (the one you’ll be getting if you buy right now) and did not have any trouble with the portafilter. You’ll also get 45 grind settings instead of the original 30, though we were hard-pressed to discern a real difference from the additional 15. —Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that ninja Luxe Cafe Premier for $600: Ninja has already released an upgraded Ninja Luxe Cafe Pro version ($750) after its espresso machine debut. But its first device, the Luxe Cafe Premier, is already a corker, a low-priced all-in-one with cold brew, coffee, espresso, excellent milk frothing, and unexpected luxury features like a built-in scale so the grinder can dose by weight. The device can feel either overstuffed or generous, depending on who you are. Either way, this damn near unseated the Breville Barista Express as WIRED’s mid-tier top pick, aside from a few leaks and sensible caution about its durability.

Sources indicate that de'Longhi La Specialista Opera for $800: Speaking of espresso makers that came running at Breville, this Opera is a beautifully forgiving semiautomatic machine that makes excellent espresso in the medium- to dark-roast range, with non-pressurized portafilter baskets that make for a nice and surprisingly subtle cup. It’s the best De'Longhi espresso machine I’ve tested, in many ways, among the semiautomatic camp. The Opera sports a lot of options—including dose and temperature control—while remaining refreshingly analog with its satisfying metal frame, metal buttons, and prominent pressure gauge. Cold brew is a perk for those who like milk. The grinder is decent, though its 15 settings might not offer enough sensitivity to pull the best from each roast. One could wish for a removable hopper and a sturdier tamping lever. But if you or your partner love cold coffee drinks or espresso martinis, this gives comparable Brevilles a strong run for the money.

De'Longhi La Specialista Touch for $800: De'Longhi’s latest Touch, released this year, isn't merely a touchscreen version of the very analog Opera—though it is just as handsome as the Opera. Instead, it offers a very specific set of trade-offs. Like De'Longhi's Rivelia, there's a bean-assist function that you can save for each bean you like. It also has a better steam wand, with the ability to read the temperature of the milk you're steaming as you steam it. In fact, it's maybe more intuitive overall. But it doesn't quite offer the easy customization on temperature, shot time, or ratios. The cold brew is not quite as well-dialed as the Opera. The Touch is an Italian machine on training wheels, designed for Italian-style medium to dark shots. This should work for most people, but minus a pressure bar or a shot timer, it can also feel like a bit of a black box.

In a recent development, la Marzocco Linea Mini for $6,600: WIRED reviewer Julian Chokkattu spent two weeks with La Marzocco's Linea Mini, a home version of the fancy espresso machines you'll see in coffee shops around the world. The price may be eye-searing, but Chokkattu did find the resulting elixir to be absolutely fantastic—and the same went for La Marzocco's customer service while Chokkattu was dialing in his machine. It offers a lot of room for experimentation, and it sports a killer cool-touch steam wand that froths milk in seconds.

It has been revealed that de'Longhi Stilosa for $150: The Stilosa was our top budget pick for years. It's still a good budget pick, and it often goes on sale for less than $100. You're not going to get high-end features like a pressure gauge or built-in grinder, and it's a little plasticky. But what the Stilosa does provide is everything you need to make great espresso at home: a solid portafilter, a reliable steam pump, and a steaming wand. It is a little light, so you'll want to brace it when you mount and dismount the portafilter (or it might slide around on you). After brewing cup after cup of espresso, the Stilosa never highlighted signs of slowing or breaking down the way many inexpensive machines can. In fact, we're now revisiting the Stilosa as our budget pick, after catching a few tips on how to use the Stilosa for light roast espresso.

Breville Barista Express Impress for $800: This espresso machine is the more tricked-out sibling of the Breville Barista Express. It includes more grind and dosing settings and automates some of the more complicated parts of brewing consistently good espresso, like getting just the right amount of beans ground per shot.

Breville Dual Boiler for $1,600: The previous-generation Breville Dual Boiler is an absolute tank of an espresso machine. It's huge. It's heavy. It makes amazing espresso. But while its size makes brewing espresso feel luxurious, it does eat up a lot of space and needs a little time to heat up, versus newer Brevilles like the Oracle Jet that favor thermoblock-style heaters. But a dual boiler does mean you can brew shot after shot, with steamed milk and hot water at the same time, without having to wait in between shots. The upcoming Breville Oracle Dual Boiler ($3,000) is already on the market, but you can still pick up the previous generation for half the price.

In a recent development, cuisinart EM-160 Slim for $250: The lowest-cost espresso maker from Cuisinart's latest espresso line is among the slimmer espresso machines out there, less than 7 inches across. This makes it a treasure for certain kitchens. The espresso quality is about what you'd expect from a pressurized portafilter: smoother, less nuanced, but also pretty forgiving for beginners trying to dial in a bean. This'll be best for those who mix milk with their espresso. Same goes for the fast-dripped “cold espresso” option, which takes a couple minutes to complete and comes out a bit tannic, but mixes well with cold milk or a lot of ice. You'll need a grinder if you don't want sad supermarket beans.

Superkop Manual Espresso Maker for $800: This manual espresso machine is technically not a Jackie Chan movie. The Superkop is instead a quite finely engineered espresso device. It looks pretty, and unlike other manual espresso machines, you don't need a strong arm to use it. So if you want to pull espresso, but not pull it hard, the Superkop is your huckleberry. That said, $600 is a lot of money for a manual device. Buy it if you know you'll love it.

Industry observers note that gevi Espresso Machine With Grinder and Milk Frother for $350: WIRED contributing reviewer Pete Cottell prized the pressure control and built-in grinder on this Gevi espresso machine, when you take into account the near-unfathomable low price for a machine with this functionality. Alas, a somewhat erratic steam wand makes it hard to recommend.

According to recent reports, cuisinart EM-640 Espresso Bar for $650: Cuisinart rolled in with some ambition on this semiautomatic espresso machine, with a built-in grinder and a non-pressurized, bottomless portafilter meant to play in the same sandbox as Breville's top devices. Alas, I really couldn't get consistency on either dosing or grinding from the device's built-in grinder—and the system for customizing the dose in particular was mostly wild guesswork. This all added up to botched shots, wild spray from the portafilter, and none of the ease one wants from a semiautomatic.

De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo for $700: This semiautomatic De'Longhi La Specialista Arte Evo comes with a built-in burr grinder and makes great espresso right out of the box, and is slimmer than other espresso machines in its category. It does have quirks: It includes a little plastic adapter needed to attach the portafilter to the grinder spout, and a little stepstool for your espresso cup to keep the coffee from splashing. It’s a good machine, but I'd upgrade to the Opera any day of the week.

Breaking: Signal to restrict screenshots over AI agent concerns – again

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (526 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set new limits on screenshots.
  • Industry observers note that whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers.
  • Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that privacy concerns around AI agents have prompted encrypted messaging app Signal to set new limits on screenshots. The organization will prevent screenshotting in its iOS 27 app and “when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android,” Signal President Meredith Whittaker wrote in a blog post Friday.

Industry observers note that whittaker noted that Google and Apple’s agentic features, including Gemini Intelligence and Siri AI’s Onscreen Awareness, compromise the privacy missions of third-party developers. These features observe what’s on a user’s screen as context for completing requests.

Also: My 5 favorite Siri AI ‘onscreen awareness’ tricks – and why.

According to recent reports, “Your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” Whittaker said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”.

Signal also blocked screenshots last year in response to Microsoft’s controversial Recall AI feature, which could capture screenshots of Signal chats on devices running Windows 11.

Signal’s move is another reminder of how Big Tech’s AI strategy trickles downstream. As AI features have moved from services external to the OS (like chatbots from OpenAI or Anthropic) to further inside of it, third-party apps have to adapt to conditions that undermine their hard-won privacy infrastructure.

Also: How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do.

Just last week, researchers at Google DeepMind used AI agents to formally verify Signal’s code, building on Signal’s own work to essentially prove the app’s encryption works. That’s a high bar for a security guarantee within the app, but it becomes meaningless if an agent can simply grab messages off a screen.

Samsung is reportedly working on its own agent, Galaxy Claw, and Apple is developing a rival for Claude and ChatGPT as well.

Whittaker noted Signal’s screenshot restriction isn’t perfect, saying that AI agents can still access app data through other means, “such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.” Earlier this week, a Reuters investigation supported by Signal and the AI Now Institute found that Meta’s Muse AI agent was using permissions from its initial setup in unexpected ways to access apps and data that a user had not explicitly connected it to.

Signal said its protections don’t right now work on MacOS.

“It is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” she added. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience.”.

If you’d still like to take screenshots, you can simply disable the setting, though Signal’s announcement strongly advised against it.

“Doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees,” Whittaker stated.

iPad Air vs iPad Pro: Which should you buy?

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro.
  • Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.
  • Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that apple’s iPad lineup is incredibly strong, and two standout options are the iPad Air and iPad Pro. If you’re trying to decide whether the iPad Pro is worth the extra cost this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

Bonus pick: The all-new iPad mini is up to $100 off for Black Friday as well.

Apple updated the iPad Air earlier this year, bringing the M4 chip for improved performance along with 12GB of RAM, up from 8GB in the previous generation.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad Air is available in 11-inch and 13-inch screen sizes, and uses an LCD display with a 60Hz refresh rate. This means it doesn’t offer OLED or ProMotion, unlike the iPad Pro. It uses Touch ID for biometric authentication, supports the Magic Keyboard and Apple Pencil Pro, and offers the full iPadOS multitasking experience.

It has been revealed that the iPad Air is available in four colors: blue, purple, starlight, and space gray. It starts at 128GB of storage and can be configured up to 1TB.

Recent findings suggest that the iPad Pro is the best iPad money can buy. It’s powered by Apple’s M5 chip and offers many advantages over the iPad Air.

Industry observers note that the biggest difference is the display technology. The iPad Pro is available in 11-inch and 13-inch sizes and uses Apple’s Ultra Retina XDR display with tandem OLED technology. This means it offers deeper blacks, better contrast, and higher brightness than the LCD screen found in the iPad Air.

It has been revealed that the iPad Pro also supports ProMotion with adaptive refresh rates up to 120Hz. This means scrolling, animations, Apple Pencil interactions, and more will be significantly smoother.

Sources indicate that contrary to what the naming implies, the iPad Pro is also noticeably thinner and lighter than the iPad Air. The 11-inch iPad Pro measures 5.3mm thick, while the 13-inch model is even thinner at 5.1mm.

The iPad Pro offers Face ID instead of Touch ID, Thunderbolt connectivity, a four-speaker audio system, and nano-texture display options with the higher-end configuration.

For most people, the iPad Air is the right choice. It delivers the entire iPad experience, excellent performance, and comes in four fun colors and two different screen sizes.

Sources indicate that the iPad Pro is the best iPad you can buy, but it’s overkill for most people. Don’t get me wrong, I love my iPad Pro. If it’s in your holiday budget, it’s a fantastic choice. I can’t overstate how impressive the tandem OLED display is. It’s significantly better than the LCD screen on the iPad Air. It’s also great having Face ID in the iPad form factor.

The iPad Pro is slightly more tempting at its current sale price, with the mid-range 13-inch model at an impressive $350 off.

Still, both the iPad Air and iPad Pro run the same iPadOS experience, and that’s why I think the iPad Air is the better value for most people. What do you think? Let us know down in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’ve ever come up against a usage limit when sending your Gemini AI assistants off to get a job done, a latest capability for Google’s artificial intelligence platform could save you the hassle — and a bunch of time in the process.
  • The company has just announced a new ‘File Slicing Controls’ feature, rolling out across all its models.
  • Though it’s primarily aimed at developers, there are elements here anyone can benefit from.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’ve ever come up against a usage limit when sending your Gemini AI assistants off to get a job done, a latest capability for Google’s artificial intelligence platform could save you the hassle — and a bunch of time in the process.

The company has just announced a new ‘File Slicing Controls’ feature, rolling out across all its models. In a nutshell, it lets you specify which elements of a file you want Gemini to focus on before it gets to work, rather than having the model do a deep scan of an entire file up front, saving you costly usage tokens in the process.

Though it’s primarily aimed at developers, there are elements here anyone can benefit from. The ‘Skim Then Zoom’ workflow is particularly useful — you can, for instance, tell the AI to summarise and explain just the text of a select range of pages in a PDF, and it’ll skim over the other pages and any associated images, just focussing on the passages you request, clawing back time and tokens.

Breaking it down, this might prove one of the most intuitively-useful updates to Gemini in a while:.

For the full run through of how the feature works, check out the Google Blog.
